_about: Error-code decoder data. Each entry explains a code in plain English. 'fix' (optional) links to a full fix page slug. Add entries any time; keep 'steps' short and safe.

stopCodes.name: IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
stopCodes.meaning: A driver tried to use memory it wasn't allowed to touch. Usually a faulty or outdated driver, sometimes unstable RAM.
steps: Update or roll back any driver you installed recently (graphics, network, audio).
Turn off XMP/EXPO or any overclock and test.
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic to check your RAM.

stopCodes.name: BAD_POOL_HEADER
stopCodes.meaning: Windows found damaged data in its shared memory. Often a bad driver, antivirus, or RAM problem.
steps: Remove or update drivers and security software installed just before this started.
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic.
Run 'sfc /scannow' in an admin Command Prompt.

stopCodes.name: MEMORY_MANAGEMENT
stopCodes.meaning: Windows hit a serious memory error. Most often unstable RAM settings (XMP/EXPO) or a failing RAM stick.
steps: Turn off XMP/EXPO in the BIOS and test.
Run a memory test such as Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86.
Update your chipset and graphics drivers.

stopCodes.name: KMODE_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
stopCodes.meaning: A driver crashed and Windows couldn't recover. The driver named on the blue screen (if any) is the main suspect.
steps: Note any .sys file named on the blue screen and update or remove that driver.
Undo recent hardware or driver changes.
Run 'sfc /scannow' in an admin Command Prompt.

stopCodes.name: NTFS_FILE_SYSTEM
stopCodes.meaning: Windows had a problem reading the drive's file system. Can mean disk errors or a failing drive.
steps: Back up important files now.
Run 'chkdsk C: /f' in an admin Command Prompt and restart.
Check the drive's health with a tool like CrystalDiskInfo.

stopCodes.name: SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION
stopCodes.meaning: A system-level program or driver crashed. Graphics drivers, antivirus, and other low-level software are common causes.
steps: Do a clean graphics driver install.
Update or remove recently installed security, RGB, or tuning software.
Run 'sfc /scannow' and then 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth'.

stopCodes.name: PFN_LIST_CORRUPT
stopCodes.meaning: Windows' list of memory pages got corrupted. Usually a bad driver or faulty RAM.
steps: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86.
Turn off XMP/EXPO and any overclock.
Update your drivers, starting with chipset and storage.

stopCodes.name: PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA
stopCodes.meaning: Windows tried to read memory that wasn't there. Common causes are faulty RAM, a bad driver, or antivirus.
steps: Run a memory test.
Turn off XMP/EXPO and test.
Update or remove drivers and security software installed right before this started.

stopCodes.name: KERNEL_STACK_INPAGE_ERROR
stopCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't read data it needed from the page file on your drive. Points to disk, cable, or RAM problems.
steps: Back up important files.
Run 'chkdsk C: /f /r' in an admin Command Prompt.
Check drive health with CrystalDiskInfo and reseat SATA cables if you have them.

stopCodes.name: KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR
stopCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't read needed data from your drive. Often a failing drive, loose cable, or RAM issue.
steps: Back up important files now.
Check drive health with CrystalDiskInfo.
Run 'chkdsk C: /f /r' and a memory test.

stopCodes.name: INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE
stopCodes.meaning: Windows lost access to the drive it boots from. Often after a BIOS change (like switching storage mode), a storage driver problem, or a failing drive.
steps: Undo recent BIOS changes, especially the SATA mode (AHCI/RAID).
Use Startup Repair from the Windows recovery screen.
Check the drive's health and connections.

stopCodes.name: SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
stopCodes.meaning: A Windows system process crashed, usually because of a driver. The .sys file named on the blue screen is the best clue.
steps: Update or roll back the driver named on the blue screen.
Do a clean graphics driver install if no driver is named.
Boot into Safe Mode if you can't start Windows normally.

stopCodes.name: UNEXPECTED_KERNEL_MODE_TRAP
stopCodes.meaning: The processor hit an error Windows couldn't handle. Often unstable overclocks, overheating, or faulty RAM.
steps: Remove all CPU, GPU, and RAM overclocks.
Check temperatures with HWiNFO.
Run a memory test.

stopCodes.name: DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE
stopCodes.meaning: A driver didn't respond when Windows changed power states, such as sleeping, waking, or shutting down.
steps: Update graphics, network, and chipset drivers.
Turn off Fast Startup in Control Panel > Power Options > Choose what the power buttons do.
Undo recent hardware or driver changes.

stopCodes.name: ATTEMPTED_WRITE_TO_READONLY_MEMORY
stopCodes.meaning: A driver tried to write to protected memory. Almost always a buggy driver.
steps: Update or remove the driver named on the blue screen, or the most recently installed one.
Run 'sfc /scannow'.
Run a memory test if it keeps happening.

stopCodes.name: BAD_POOL_CALLER
stopCodes.meaning: A driver made a bad memory request. Usually a buggy driver or security software.
steps: Update or remove recently installed drivers and antivirus.
Run 'sfc /scannow'.
Run a memory test.

stopCodes.name: DRIVER_CORRUPTED_EXPOOL
stopCodes.meaning: A driver damaged Windows' shared memory. Usually a buggy driver.
steps: Update or remove the most recently installed drivers.
Run a memory test.
Run 'sfc /scannow'.

stopCodes.name: DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
stopCodes.meaning: A driver accessed memory it shouldn't have. Network, Wi-Fi, and graphics drivers are frequent culprits. Check the .sys file named on the blue screen.
steps: Update the driver named on the blue screen (for example, a network driver).
Do a clean graphics driver install.
Turn off XMP/EXPO if it keeps happening.

stopCodes.name: UNMOUNTABLE_BOOT_VOLUME
stopCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't open the drive it starts from. Could be file system damage or a failing drive.
steps: From the recovery screen, open Command Prompt and run 'chkdsk C: /f /r'.
Try Startup Repair.
Back up data and check drive health as soon as you can.

stopCodes.name: CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED
stopCodes.meaning: A process Windows can't run without stopped unexpectedly. Often damaged system files, a bad driver, or a failing drive.
steps: Run 'sfc /scannow' and then 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' in an admin Command Prompt.
Undo recent updates or driver changes, or use System Restore.
Check your drive's health.

stopCodes.name: CRITICAL_OBJECT_TERMINATION
stopCodes.meaning: An essential Windows process ended unexpectedly, frequently because the drive stopped responding.
steps: Back up important files.
Check drive health and update your storage (SSD/NVMe) firmware.
Run 'chkdsk C: /f' and 'sfc /scannow'.

stopCodes.name: ATTEMPTED_EXECUTE_OF_NOEXECUTE_MEMORY
stopCodes.meaning: A driver tried to run code from memory marked as data-only. Usually a buggy driver.
steps: Update or remove recently installed drivers.
Run a memory test.
Run 'sfc /scannow'.

stopCodes.name: CLOCK_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
stopCodes.meaning: One of your CPU cores stopped responding. Often an unstable CPU overclock or undervolt, overheating, or a BIOS issue.
steps: Reset CPU overclocks and undervolts to default in the BIOS.
Check CPU temperatures with HWiNFO.
Update your BIOS and chipset drivers.

stopCodes.name: CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION
stopCodes.meaning: Windows detected that its core code or data was changed. Usually a driver, cheat/anti-cheat software, or faulty RAM.
steps: Uninstall recently added drivers, tools, or software that hooks into Windows.
Run a memory test.
Run 'sfc /scannow'.

stopCodes.name: VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE
stopCodes.meaning: Your graphics card stopped responding and Windows couldn't reset it.
steps: Do a clean graphics driver install with DDU.
Remove GPU overclocks.
Check GPU temperatures and power cables.

stopCodes.name: VIDEO_TDR_TIMEOUT_DETECTED
stopCodes.meaning: Your graphics card stopped responding for a moment and Windows reset the driver.
steps: Do a clean graphics driver install.
Remove GPU overclocks.
Check GPU temperatures and power cables.

stopCodes.name: WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR
stopCodes.meaning: Your hardware reported an error it couldn't fix. Common causes are unstable overclocks (including XMP/EXPO), overheating, or failing hardware.
steps: Reset all overclocks and turn off XMP/EXPO.
Check temperatures with HWiNFO.
Update your BIOS and chipset drivers.

stopCodes.name: DPC_WATCHDOG_VIOLATION
stopCodes.meaning: A driver took too long to respond. Storage (SSD/NVMe) drivers and firmware are frequent causes.
steps: Update your SSD/NVMe firmware and storage drivers.
Update chipset drivers from AMD or Intel.
Undo recent driver changes.

stopCodes.name: KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE
stopCodes.meaning: Windows detected corrupted data inside the kernel. Usually unstable RAM settings or a bad driver.
steps: Turn off XMP/EXPO and test.
Run a memory test.
Update chipset and GPU drivers.

stopCodes.name: KERNEL_MODE_HEAP_CORRUPTION
stopCodes.meaning: A driver corrupted Windows' memory. Often a graphics or other recently updated driver.
steps: Do a clean graphics driver install, or roll back to the previous version.
Update or remove recently installed drivers.
Run a memory test.

stopCodes.name: UNEXPECTED_STORE_EXCEPTION
stopCodes.meaning: Windows' memory compression store hit an error. Often a drive, storage driver, or RAM problem.
steps: Check drive health and update SSD firmware.
Run 'chkdsk C: /f' and 'sfc /scannow'.
Run a memory test.

exceptionCodes.name: Access violation
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program tried to use memory it wasn't allowed to. This is the most common app and game crash code. The cause is usually something loaded into the program: a mod, overlay, antivirus, or a graphics driver.
steps: Check which module crashed (look for 'Faulting module' in Event Viewer) — this tells you whose code failed.
Turn off overlays (Steam, Discord, NVIDIA, RivaTuner) and remove mods.
Update or clean-install your graphics driver, then verify or reinstall the program.

exceptionCodes.name: In-page error
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program couldn't read part of itself from the drive. Often a drive problem, or the program is on a disconnected or sleeping drive.
steps: Make sure the drive with the program is connected and healthy.
Run 'chkdsk' on that drive.
Reinstall the program.

exceptionCodes.name: Out of memory
exceptionCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't give the program the memory it asked for.
steps: Close other programs.
Set virtual memory (page file) back to 'Automatically manage'.
Make sure your drive has free space.

exceptionCodes.name: Illegal instruction
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program used a processor instruction your CPU doesn't support, or the CPU is unstable.
steps: Check that your CPU meets the program's requirements.
Remove any CPU overclock or undervolt.
Update the program to its latest version.

exceptionCodes.name: Access denied
exceptionCodes.meaning: Windows blocked the program from a file or resource. Often permissions or antivirus.
steps: Check your antivirus quarantine and add the program's folder to exclusions.
Make sure the program isn't installed in a protected or synced folder.
Repair or reinstall the program.

exceptionCodes.name: Invalid image format
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program found a file built for the wrong system type (for example, a 32-bit file where a 64-bit one was needed). Almost always broken or mismatched Visual C++, DirectX, or program files.
steps: Install both the x64 and x86 versions of the latest Visual C++ Redistributable from Microsoft.
Install the DirectX End-User Runtime from Microsoft.
Verify or reinstall the program. Don't copy DLLs from other PCs or DLL websites.

exceptionCodes.name: DLL not found
exceptionCodes.meaning: A file the program needs is missing. Often a missing runtime such as Visual C++ or .NET.
steps: Install the latest Visual C++ Redistributable (x64 and x86) from Microsoft.
Install the .NET runtime the program asks for from Microsoft.
Repair or reinstall the program.

exceptionCodes.name: DLL initialization failed
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program failed while starting up its supporting files. Can be damaged runtimes, security software, or system file problems.
steps: Restart your PC.
Repair the Visual C++ Redistributables in Apps > Installed apps.
Run 'sfc /scannow' and check your antivirus quarantine.

exceptionCodes.name: Stack overflow
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program got stuck in a loop and ran out of a type of memory. This is usually a bug in the program or a mod.
steps: Update the program.
Remove mods or plugins.
Report it to the program's developer if it keeps happening.

exceptionCodes.name: Heap corruption
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program damaged its own memory. Often a bug, a mod, an overlay, or unstable RAM.
steps: Remove mods and turn off overlays.
Update the program and your graphics driver.
Turn off XMP/EXPO and run a memory test if many programs crash this way.

exceptionCodes.name: Stack buffer overrun
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program stopped itself after detecting a serious internal error. Often an outdated program, a bad mod, overlay, or damaged files.
steps: Update the program and verify its files.
Turn off overlays and remove mods.
Update your graphics driver.

exceptionCodes.name: Fatal user callback exception
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program crashed while Windows was handing it a message. Often overlays, hooks, or compatibility settings.
steps: Turn off overlays and screen recorders.
Turn off compatibility mode in the program's Properties > Compatibility.
Update the program.

exceptionCodes.name: Fatal app exit
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program closed itself after an error it couldn't handle. Often missing or damaged files.
steps: Verify or reinstall the program.
Repair the Visual C++ Redistributables.
Check antivirus quarantine.

exceptionCodes.name: Breakpoint
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program hit a deliberate stop point, usually a built-in crash check. The real cause is often damaged files, settings, or the graphics setup.
steps: Verify the program's files.
Reset its settings (rename its settings folder in Documents or AppData).
Update your graphics driver.

exceptionCodes.name: C++ exception
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program threw an internal error it didn't handle. The cause depends on the program; it's often a missing file, bad setting, or bug.
steps: Update and verify the program.
Reset its settings.
Check the program's own log files for a more specific message.

exceptionCodes.name: DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED
exceptionCodes.meaning: The program lost contact with your graphics card.
steps: Remove GPU overclocks.
Do a clean graphics driver install.
Check GPU power cables and temperatures.

exceptionCodes.name: DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG
exceptionCodes.meaning: Your graphics card stopped responding to the program.
steps: Remove GPU overclocks.
Do a clean graphics driver install.
Check GPU temperatures.

exceptionCodes.name: DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_RESET
exceptionCodes.meaning: The graphics card was reset, often after bad commands or a driver problem.
steps: Do a clean graphics driver install.
Remove GPU overclocks.
Update the program.

updateCodes.name: File not found
updateCodes.meaning: Windows Update couldn't find files it needed, often after an interrupted download.
steps: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter (Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters).
Restart and try the update again.
Run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' then 'sfc /scannow'.

updateCodes.name: Access denied
updateCodes.meaning: Windows or an installer didn't have permission to change something. Often security software or permissions.
steps: Make sure you're signed in as an administrator.
Temporarily pause third-party antivirus, update, then turn it back on.
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter.

updateCodes.name: Not enough disk space
updateCodes.meaning: There isn't enough free space to install the update.
steps: Free up space with Settings > System > Storage > Temporary files.
Uninstall programs you don't use.
Try again once you have at least 20 GB free.

updateCodes.name: Invalid data
updateCodes.meaning: Update files were damaged or unreadable.
steps: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter.
Run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' then 'sfc /scannow'.
Try the update again.

updateCodes.name: Update service disabled
updateCodes.meaning: The Windows Update service is turned off, often by a 'debloat' or tweaking tool.
steps: Press Windows+R, type 'services.msc', and set 'Windows Update' to Manual or Automatic, then Start it.
Undo changes made by tweaking or debloat tools.
Try the update again.

updateCodes.name: Install failed
updateCodes.meaning: A component failed to install. On recent Windows versions this sometimes relates to a security update for the recovery partition.
steps: Restart and try again.
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter.
Search Microsoft's support site for the update's KB number for specific guidance.

updateCodes.name: Timed out
updateCodes.meaning: The update or operation took too long and gave up.
steps: Check your internet connection and restart your router.
Restart your PC and try again.
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter.

updateCodes.name: Component store damaged
updateCodes.meaning: Files Windows uses to install updates are damaged.
steps: Run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' in an admin Command Prompt.
Run 'sfc /scannow'.
Restart and try the update again.

updateCodes.name: Source files not found
updateCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't find files needed to install a feature or update, often .NET Framework 3.5.
steps: Run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth'.
Make sure Windows Update isn't blocked by policy or tools.
Install the feature through Settings > System > Optional features or Windows Features.

updateCodes.name: Couldn't finish installing
updateCodes.meaning: The update failed to complete, often due to connection problems, a VPN, or a full system partition.
steps: Disconnect from any VPN and try again.
Check your internet connection.
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter.

updateCodes.name: Can't reach update servers
updateCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't connect to Microsoft's update servers. Often proxy, DNS, or firewall settings.
steps: Turn off any proxy or VPN.
Switch to a public DNS (1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8).
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter.

updateCodes.name: Download failed
steps: Restart and try again.
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter.
Free up disk space and check your connection.

updateCodes.name: Upgrade rolled back (driver)
updateCodes.meaning: A Windows feature upgrade failed and rolled back, usually because of a driver or connected device.
steps: Unplug extra USB devices (drives, adapters, controllers).
Update all drivers, especially storage, graphics, and network.
Uninstall third-party antivirus during the upgrade.

updateCodes.name: Unspecified error
updateCodes.meaning: A general error with no specific reason. The surrounding message usually says more.
steps: Restart and try again.
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter if it's an update.
Look for a more specific error message or code nearby.

updateCodes.name: I/O device error
updateCodes.meaning: Windows had trouble reading or writing to a drive or device.
steps: Back up important files.
Check the drive's connection and health.
Run 'chkdsk' on the affected drive.

deviceCodes.name: Device cannot start
deviceCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't start this device, usually a driver problem.
steps: Update or reinstall the device's driver from the manufacturer's site.
Unplug and reconnect the device, or try another port.
Restart your PC.

deviceCodes.name: Drivers not installed
deviceCodes.meaning: No driver is installed for this device.
steps: Download the driver from the device or motherboard maker's site.
Run Windows Update, including Optional updates.
Restart after installing.

deviceCodes.name: Device not working properly
deviceCodes.meaning: Windows couldn't load the driver for this device.
steps: Uninstall the device in Device Manager and restart.
Install the latest driver from the manufacturer.
Check for Windows updates.

deviceCodes.name: Driver missing or corrupted
deviceCodes.meaning: Windows can't load the device's driver; it may be damaged or missing.
steps: Reinstall the driver from the manufacturer's site.
Uninstall the device in Device Manager and restart.
Run 'sfc /scannow'.

deviceCodes.name: Device reported problems
deviceCodes.meaning: Windows stopped the device because it reported a problem. For graphics cards and USB devices this can be a driver, power, or hardware issue.
steps: Do a clean install of the device's driver (DDU for graphics cards).
Reseat the device or try another port and cable.
Test it in another PC if possible to rule out hardware failure.

deviceCodes.name: Device not connected
deviceCodes.meaning: The device was connected before but isn't now.
steps: Reconnect the device.
Try a different port or cable.
Ignore it if you removed the device on purpose.

deviceCodes.name: Driver signature problem
deviceCodes.meaning: Windows can't verify the driver's signature, so it won't load it.
steps: Download the official driver from the manufacturer.
Run Windows Update.
Avoid drivers from unofficial download sites.

dlls.name: Visual C++ 2015–2022 Redistributable
dlls.meaning: This file comes with Microsoft's Visual C++ Redistributable, which many programs and games need.
steps: Download the latest Visual C++ Redistributable from Microsoft's website.
Install both the x64 and the x86 versions, then restart.
Still missing? Repair it in Apps > Installed apps, and check your antivirus quarantine.

dlls.name: Visual C++ 2013 Redistributable
dlls.meaning: This file comes with the older Visual C++ 2013 Redistributable.
steps: Download the Visual C++ 2013 Redistributable from Microsoft's website.
Install both the x64 and x86 versions, then restart.

dlls.name: Visual C++ 2012 Redistributable
dlls.meaning: This file comes with the older Visual C++ 2012 Redistributable.
steps: Download the Visual C++ 2012 Redistributable from Microsoft's website.
Install both the x64 and x86 versions, then restart.

dlls.name: Visual C++ 2010 Redistributable
dlls.meaning: This file comes with the older Visual C++ 2010 Redistributable.
steps: Download the Visual C++ 2010 Redistributable from Microsoft's website.
Install both the x64 and x86 versions, then restart.

dlls.name: DirectX End-User Runtime
dlls.meaning: Older games need extra DirectX files that Windows doesn't include by default.
steps: Download the 'DirectX End-User Runtime Web Installer' from Microsoft's website and run it.
Restart and launch the game again.

dlls.name: Steam game file
dlls.meaning: This file belongs to the game itself. If it's missing, your antivirus probably quarantined it or the install is damaged.
steps: Check your antivirus quarantine and restore the file.
Add the game folder to your antivirus exclusions.
Verify the game files in Steam.

dlls.name: Windows Media Feature Pack
dlls.meaning: Windows 'N' editions don't include media features some games and apps need.
steps: Go to Settings > System > Optional features > Add a feature.
Install 'Media Feature Pack' and restart.

dlls.name: Games for Windows Live
dlls.meaning: This game uses Microsoft's discontinued Games for Windows Live service.
steps: Check the store page or community guides for a patched version of the game.
Don't download xlive.dll from DLL websites.

modules.name: NVIDIA graphics driver
modules.meaning: The crash happened inside NVIDIA's graphics driver.
steps: Do a clean install of the latest NVIDIA driver (or the previous version if this started after an update).
Remove any GPU overclock.
Turn off overlays such as the NVIDIA App overlay.

modules.name: AMD graphics driver
modules.meaning: The crash happened inside AMD's graphics driver.
steps: Do a clean install of the latest AMD driver with AMD's Cleanup Utility or DDU.
Remove any GPU overclock or undervolt in AMD Software.
Turn off AMD overlays and features like Radeon Anti-Lag for a test.

modules.name: Intel graphics driver
modules.meaning: The crash happened inside Intel's graphics driver.
steps: Update your Intel graphics driver from Intel's website or your PC maker's site.
On a laptop with a second graphics card, make sure the program runs on the dedicated card (Settings > System > Display > Graphics).

modules.name: Windows core (ntdll.dll)
modules.meaning: ntdll.dll is a core Windows file that's involved in almost every crash, so it's rarely the real cause. Something else, such as a mod, overlay, damaged file, or unstable RAM, usually broke the program first.
steps: Look for other module or file names in the crash report.
Turn off overlays and remove mods.
Verify or reinstall the program, and run a memory test if many programs crash.

modules.name: Windows error handler (KERNELBASE.dll)
modules.meaning: KERNELBASE.dll is where Windows reports a program's own internal error. The program itself hit a problem, often missing files, bad settings, or a bug.
steps: Update and verify the program.
Reset its settings.
Repair the Visual C++ Redistributables and .NET runtime.

modules.name: .NET runtime
modules.meaning: The crash happened in Microsoft's .NET runtime, which the program is built on.
steps: Install the latest .NET runtime the program requires from Microsoft.
Repair or reinstall the program.
Run Windows Update.

modules.name: DirectX
modules.meaning: The crash happened in DirectX, the graphics layer between the game and your GPU driver. If this file is inside the game's own folder, it's probably a mod like ReShade, not the real DirectX.
steps: Check the game's folder for a dxgi.dll, d3d11.dll or d3d9.dll file. If you have one, it's a mod (often ReShade); remove it to test.
Update your graphics driver.
Turn off overlays.

modules.name: Vulkan
modules.meaning: The crash happened in the Vulkan graphics layer.
steps: Update your graphics driver.
Turn off overlays, which often hook into Vulkan.
Try the game's DirectX mode instead.

modules.name: RivaTuner overlay
modules.meaning: RivaTuner (often installed with MSI Afterburner) was hooked into the program when it crashed.
steps: Close RivaTuner/Afterburner and test.
Update RivaTuner, or add the program to its exclusions.

modules.name: Steam overlay
modules.meaning: The Steam overlay was hooked into the program when it crashed.
steps: Turn off the Steam overlay for this game (right-click the game > Properties > General).
Test again.

modules.name: Discord overlay
modules.meaning: Discord's in-game overlay was hooked into the program when it crashed.
steps: Turn off Discord's in-game overlay (User Settings > Game Overlay).
Test again.

modules.name: OBS game capture
modules.meaning: OBS's game capture hook was inside the program when it crashed.
steps: Switch OBS to Window Capture or Display Capture for this game.
Update OBS.

modules.name: NVIDIA overlay / recording
modules.meaning: NVIDIA's overlay or recording feature was hooked into the program when it crashed.
steps: Turn off the NVIDIA App overlay.
Test again, then update the NVIDIA App.

modules.name: ReShade
modules.meaning: The ReShade graphics mod was loaded when the program crashed.
steps: Remove or update ReShade.
Turn off heavy shaders and test again.

modules.name: Bitdefender
modules.meaning: Bitdefender's monitoring was hooked into the program when it crashed.
steps: Add the program's folder to Bitdefender's exceptions, including Advanced Threat Defense.
Test again.

modules.name: Avast / AVG
modules.meaning: Avast or AVG antivirus was hooked into the program when it crashed.
steps: Add the program's folder to the antivirus exceptions.
Test again.

phrases.name: Kernel-Power Event 41
phrases.meaning: Windows restarted without shutting down properly. It doesn't say why; common causes are power problems, overheating, unstable overclocks, or a blue screen that didn't get saved.
steps: Check for a blue screen code in Event Viewer around the same time (look for 'BugCheck').
Remove overclocks and check temperatures.
Check power: the power supply, cables, and power strip.

phrases.name: LiveKernelEvent
phrases.meaning: Windows recorded a hardware or driver problem it recovered from. Codes 141 and 117 usually mean the graphics card stopped responding.
steps: Do a clean graphics driver install.
Remove GPU overclocks.
Check GPU temperatures and power cables.

match: your pc ran into a problem
your device ran into a problem
phrases.name: Blue screen
phrases.meaning: Windows had to stop to protect itself. The stop code on the screen tells you why.
steps: Find the stop code: it's on the blue screen, or in Event Viewer > Windows Logs > System (look for 'BugCheck').
Paste that stop code here to decode it.

match: is not a valid win32 application
this app can't run on your pc
phrases.name: Incompatible program
phrases.meaning: The program wasn't built for your version or type of Windows, or the file is damaged.
steps: Download the correct version for your Windows (64-bit, 32-bit, or ARM).
Re-download the installer in case the file is damaged.
Check the program's system requirements.

phrases.name: Application hang
phrases.meaning: The program froze and Windows closed it.
steps: Update the program and your graphics driver.
Turn off overlays and close background programs.
Check that your drive and antivirus aren't slowing it down.

match: the system has recovered from a serious error
phrases.name: Recovered from a blue screen
phrases.meaning: Windows restarted after a blue screen.
steps: Look for the 'BugCheck' entry in Event Viewer > Windows Logs > System, or check C:\Windows\Minidump.
Paste the stop code here to decode it.
